articles.title: 'Ladrão aí, ó': entregadores filmaram e acusaram Cláudio Rafael de roubo antes de linchamento em Copacabana | G1
articles.standfirst: Imagens de câmeras de segurança e a investigação da polícia ajudam a reconstruir os últimos momentos de Claudio Rafael Landeiro, morto após uma sequência de agressões na Zona Sul do Rio.
articles.summary: Imagens de câmeras de segurança e a investigação da polícia ajudam a reconstruir os últimos momentos de Claudio Rafael Landeiro, morto após uma sequência de agressões na Zona Sul do Rio.
articles.body:
Cláudio Rafael Landeiro, de 37 anos, foi filmado e chamado de “ladrão” pelos entregadores Felipe Eduardo dos Santos Silva e Ailton José da Silva pouco antes de ser espancado até a morte em Copacabana , na Zona Sul do Rio de Janeiro . Segundo a investigação, eles haviam sido avisados de que havia um suposto ladrão de bicicleta na região.

As imagens mostram Rafael sentado na escadaria de um prédio quando os entregadores chegam. Eles tiram os celulares e passam a filmá-lo.

“Ladrão aí, ó. Tiver roubando aqui na Zona Sul, nós 'vai' dar uma coça, nós vai matar, mano", diz um dos entregadores no vídeo.

Logo depois, começam as agressões. Um homem não identificado aparece e dá um chute em Rafael. Davi Santos Machado, um dos seguranças envolvidos no caso, chega ao local e passa a golpeá-lo com um pedaço de pau. Rafael também é atingido por socos e chutes.

Segundo a polícia, o linchamento durou cerca de nove minutos. Rafael levou 63 pauladas.

Entregadores filmaram Cláudio Rafael antes de começarem espancamento que levou homem à morte. — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo/Fantástico

Mas, antes de ser perseguido e agredido, Rafael havia passado por uma loja de conveniência em Copacabana, quando foi abordado pelo segurança Davi.

Na noite de 11 de agosto, ele saiu de casa, em Botafogo, para dar uma volta na bicicleta da irmã. Às 22h54, chegou à loja. Entrou para pedir um cigarro avulso, mas deixou o estabelecimento depois de ouvir que precisaria pagar.

Às 23h21, Davi aparece conversando com Rafael na entrada da loja. Segundo a investigação, ele perguntou de quem era a bicicleta.

“Conversa que a gente teve foi só essa pergunta, só perguntando se a bicicleta era dele ou não. A gente perguntou isso umas três vezes, ele respondeu que não era”, contou um funcionário da loja, que preferiu não se identificar.

Entregadores abordam Rafael e o acusam de ladrão em um vídeo. — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo/Fantástico

A bicicleta foi presa com um cadeado junto a galões de água. Davi tirou fotos do veículo e, depois, disse ao funcionário que havia encontrado o dono.

Ainda segundo a investigação, Davi chamou outro segurança, Jorge Luiz Ricardo Dias. As câmeras mostram Jorge levando a bicicleta enquanto Rafael tenta impedir que ele vá embora com o veículo.

Davi aparece depois com um porrete, ataca Rafael e o persegue.

Perto da meia-noite, entregadores que costumavam ficar em uma esquina aguardando pedidos foram avisados sobre a presença de um suposto ladrão de bicicleta.

“Aí chamaram, falaram que tinha agarrado um ladrão ali, segurança tinha agarrado o ladrão ali, tá ligado?”, contou um entregador ouvido pela reportagem.

Felipe e Ailton chegaram ao local onde Rafael havia sido visto. Segundo a investigação, Davi informou aos dois que o suposto ladrão havia acabado de passar.

Os dois passaram a seguir Rafael. Ele dobrou em uma rua e se sentou na escadaria de um prédio.

Em vídeo, os entregadores ameaçam Cláudio Rafael. — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo/Fantástico

Foi nesse momento que os entregadores chegaram, filmaram Rafael e o chamaram de “ladrão”.

Depois das agressões, Rafael permaneceu no chão e ficou cerca de 30 minutos aguardando o socorro.

“Ele estava agonizando no chão, tentando levantar até que o corpo de bombeiro chegou. Ele foi socorrido, mas infelizmente ele veio a falecer", disse o delegado Ângelo Lages, da Polícia Civil, responsável pela investigação.

Quatro pessoas foram presas pela morte: os seguranças Davi Santos Machado e Jorge Luiz Ricardo Dias e os entregadores Felipe Eduardo dos Santos Silva e Ailton José da Silva .

Os seguranças e Felipe confessaram o crime. Ailton ficou em silêncio durante o depoimento à polícia.

As imagens de câmeras de segurança da região estão sendo usadas pela polícia para esclarecer a dinâmica do crime. A investigação também pretende identificar pessoas que presenciaram as agressões.

“Todas as pessoas que presenciaram essa cena, que estiveram ali, a gente vai identificá-las, a gente pretende ouvi-las, até porque elas podem responder pelo crime de omissão de socorro", afirma o delegado.

paragraphs: Cláudio Rafael Landeiro, de 37 anos, foi filmado e chamado de “ladrão” pelos entregadores Felipe Eduardo dos Santos Silva e Ailton José da Silva pouco antes de ser espancado até a morte em Copacabana , na Zona Sul do Rio de Janeiro . Segundo a investigação, eles haviam sido avisados de que havia um suposto ladrão de bicicleta na região.
As imagens mostram Rafael sentado na escadaria de um prédio quando os entregadores chegam. Eles tiram os celulares e passam a filmá-lo.
“Ladrão aí, ó. Tiver roubando aqui na Zona Sul, nós 'vai' dar uma coça, nós vai matar, mano", diz um dos entregadores no vídeo.

Logo depois, começam as agressões. Um homem não identificado aparece e dá um chute em Rafael. Davi Santos Machado, um dos seguranças envolvidos no caso, chega ao local e passa a golpeá-lo com um pedaço de pau. Rafael também é atingido por socos e chutes.
Segundo a polícia, o linchamento durou cerca de nove minutos. Rafael levou 63 pauladas.
Entregadores filmaram Cláudio Rafael antes de começarem espancamento que levou homem à morte. — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo/Fantástico
Mas, antes de ser perseguido e agredido, Rafael havia passado por uma loja de conveniência em Copacabana, quando foi abordado pelo segurança Davi.

Na noite de 11 de agosto, ele saiu de casa, em Botafogo, para dar uma volta na bicicleta da irmã. Às 22h54, chegou à loja. Entrou para pedir um cigarro avulso, mas deixou o estabelecimento depois de ouvir que precisaria pagar.
Às 23h21, Davi aparece conversando com Rafael na entrada da loja. Segundo a investigação, ele perguntou de quem era a bicicleta.

“Conversa que a gente teve foi só essa pergunta, só perguntando se a bicicleta era dele ou não. A gente perguntou isso umas três vezes, ele respondeu que não era”, contou um funcionário da loja, que preferiu não se identificar.
Entregadores abordam Rafael e o acusam de ladrão em um vídeo. — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo/Fantástico
A bicicleta foi presa com um cadeado junto a galões de água. Davi tirou fotos do veículo e, depois, disse ao funcionário que havia encontrado o dono.
Ainda segundo a investigação, Davi chamou outro segurança, Jorge Luiz Ricardo Dias. As câmeras mostram Jorge levando a bicicleta enquanto Rafael tenta impedir que ele vá embora com o veículo.
Davi aparece depois com um porrete, ataca Rafael e o persegue.
Perto da meia-noite, entregadores que costumavam ficar em uma esquina aguardando pedidos foram avisados sobre a presença de um suposto ladrão de bicicleta.
“Aí chamaram, falaram que tinha agarrado um ladrão ali, segurança tinha agarrado o ladrão ali, tá ligado?”, contou um entregador ouvido pela reportagem.
Felipe e Ailton chegaram ao local onde Rafael havia sido visto. Segundo a investigação, Davi informou aos dois que o suposto ladrão havia acabado de passar.
Os dois passaram a seguir Rafael. Ele dobrou em uma rua e se sentou na escadaria de um prédio.
Em vídeo, os entregadores ameaçam Cláudio Rafael. — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo/Fantástico
Foi nesse momento que os entregadores chegaram, filmaram Rafael e o chamaram de “ladrão”.
Depois das agressões, Rafael permaneceu no chão e ficou cerca de 30 minutos aguardando o socorro.

“Ele estava agonizando no chão, tentando levantar até que o corpo de bombeiro chegou. Ele foi socorrido, mas infelizmente ele veio a falecer", disse o delegado Ângelo Lages, da Polícia Civil, responsável pela investigação.
Quatro pessoas foram presas pela morte: os seguranças Davi Santos Machado e Jorge Luiz Ricardo Dias e os entregadores Felipe Eduardo dos Santos Silva e Ailton José da Silva .
Os seguranças e Felipe confessaram o crime. Ailton ficou em silêncio durante o depoimento à polícia.
As imagens de câmeras de segurança da região estão sendo usadas pela polícia para esclarecer a dinâmica do crime. A investigação também pretende identificar pessoas que presenciaram as agressões.

“Todas as pessoas que presenciaram essa cena, que estiveram ali, a gente vai identificá-las, a gente pretende ouvi-las, até porque elas podem responder pelo crime de omissão de socorro", afirma o delegado.

articles.title: NHS failing child sex abuse victims, say psychiatrists
articles.summary: There have been decades of mistreatment and mismanagement of those who seek help later in life, say experts in a new, damning report.
articles.body:
People sexually abused as children who seek help in later life for mental health problems are being failed by the NHS, senior doctors have told the BBC.

The Royal College of Psychiatrists is issuing a public apology for what it says is decades of mismanagement and misdiagnosis in the UK.

For some, it has worsened their traumas, it said.

The college said mental health staff have been too focussed on treating symptoms rather than exploring how past traumatic experiences can still affect patients.

Support is improving, it said, but there must be better training and more investment - something NHS bosses have said is being introduced.

The apology has been included in a report by the college and given to the BBC.

Immediate past president of the college, Dr Lade Smith, said she was "sorry" that, too often, victims have suffered "avoidable harm when seeking help".

The report details how treatment has sometimes been inappropriate, while people have been re-traumatised by the experience of repeated assessments and history-taking and not always being believed.

Dr Smith told the BBC it was clear people were not getting the support they needed, and that this was not just a failing of psychiatrists, but the whole mental health system.

"Services are so fragmented. The system is set up to provide short, discreet episodes of care. Psychiatrists do not get the time to build up a relationship with patients so they can be properly supported.

"They are lucky if they get eight sessions of therapy, when it could take eight sessions for a person just to disclose the abuse.

"And these are just the people who get support – many don't even get seen by mental health services because services are so stretched," she said.

Estimates suggest nearly one in 10 adults in England and Wales were abused in childhood.

Such trauma increases the risk of mental health problems, including alcohol and drug misuse, eating disorders, self-harm, complex PTSD, anxiety and depression.

Many struggle to talk about the abuse. Around two-thirds of those abused as children have not disclosed it to services by the time they reach adulthood.

One in five never disclose, and many of those that do take decades to speak out.

Caroline Thompson, 65, is someone who feels let down by the NHS.

She was psychologically and sexually abused when she was a child.

She went on to raise a family and have a successful career as a specialist ear, nose and throat doctor.

It was not until she started experiencing terrifying nightmares, aged 55, that left her unable to function due to mental exhaustion and lack of sleep, that she realised she needed help and was referred to mental health services.

The psychiatrist she saw said her symptoms were unlikely to be due to the abuse because of the delay in presentation and given she had been able to have a family and successful career. She was diagnosed with anxiety and given anti-psychotic drugs.

"I had therapy for about a year and was then discharged. At that point I still didn't understand what was happening to me and I still couldn't function due to the nightmares and side-effects of the drugs. I had to give up the job I loved."

Caroline then got private therapy with a therapist who specialised in childhood trauma and gradually began to get better over the next few years.

She says: "It was astonishing to me that it was not understood that traumatic memories are buried in order for you to survive, and that those memories can surface years later. So any delay in presenting is quite normal."

The apology comes after the college set up a working group of experts, doctors and abuse survivors, including Caroline and chaired by leading consultant psychiatrists Jo Stubley and Maria Podlejska-Eyres, to review NHS care.

The group was set up after mental health services have seen a rise in people coming forward seeking help in the last decade or so, following high-profile abuse scandals involving schools, children's homes and religious institutions, as well as the Jimmy Savile crimes .

The college is calling for a number of changes. It is promising to develop specialist training materials for psychiatrists, but wants mandatory training for all mental health staff on the importance of trauma-informed care for survivors of child sex abuse.

And it has recommended national guidance be published on how to recognise and respond to disclosures of historic child sex abuse, as well as an overhaul of services so those needing help can get the long-term support they need.

Gabrielle Shaw, chief executive of the National Association for People Abused in Childhood, said this was a "significant and welcome" apology, but it must lead to "meaningful change".

"For too many adult survivors, mental health services have not felt like a route to safety or recovery."

A spokesman for NHS England said specialist services were available, highlighting how victims could access support 24 hours a day, seven days a week through sexual assault referral centres and counselling services with information about them available on the NHS website .

"People who have suffered historic child sexual abuse may not have spoken about it for years, so it's vital they know they can access specialist, trauma-informed support through the NHS," he added.

He also said steps were being taken to better support children and young people with additional training being provided to mental health support teams in schools and colleges.

If you've been affected by the issues in this story, you can find information, advice and support from the BBC's Action Line . Anyone feeling emotionally distressed or suicidal can call Samaritans for free on 116 123 or visit samaritans.org in the UK.

articles.title: âSecure, predictable sea lanes indispensableâ: India urges UN to safeguard key maritime routes
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: India has called on the international community to work collectively to safeguard critical sea lanes and maritime infrastructure, saying se.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India has called on the international community to work collectively to safeguard critical sea lanes and maritime infrastructure, saying secure and predictable shipping routes are essential to ensure the uninterrupted movement of food, fertilisers, fuel and other vital commodities amid conflicts and growing disruptions to global supply chains.Speaking at a UN Security Council high-level open debate on Tuesday on the theme âFood Under Fire: The Security Council's Role in Mitigating Global and Local Food Crisesâ, Indiaâs Permanent Representative to the UN, Ambassador Harish Parvathaneni, said regional conflicts were increasingly producing consequences far beyond the immediate theatres of hostilities.âSecure and predictable maritime trade routes are indispensable for the uninterrupted movement of food, fertilisers, fuel and other essential commodities," Parvathaneni said, underscoring the need to preserve the safety and freedom of navigation for commercial shipping in accordance with international law.The call comes as conflicts and attacks on key maritime routes continue to threaten global food and energy supplies. UN secretary general Antonio Guterres told the Council that the Strait of Hormuz carries around a fifth of global oil supplies and a third of global fertiliser trade.âRestrictions and closures have driven up commodity prices and made availability plummet. And attacks on commercial vessels in the Red Sea are further threatening supply chains for food and other commodities,â Guterres said.Parvathaneni warned that disruptions to commercial shipping during conflicts could have cascading effects well beyond the affected region, with food-importing developing countries and humanitarian operations bearing a disproportionate burden.âThe international community must therefore work collectively to safeguard critical sea lanes and maritime infrastructure, while ensuring that legitimate commercial trade and humanitarian shipments are able to proceed without undue impediment,â he said.India said the immediate priority for the Security Council should be to reduce the humanitarian consequences of conflicts by facilitating safe, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access, supporting de-confliction arrangements where appropriate and ensuring that Council measures, including sanctions regimes, do not inadvertently obstruct humanitarian assistance or legitimate food and agricultural trade.Parvathaneni also called for timely assessments of disruptions to critical supply chains covering food, fertiliser, fuel and humanitarian logistics, drawing on the expertise of the food and agriculture organisation, the World Food Programme and other relevant agencies.âSuch assessments must remain objective, evidence-based and free from politicisation,â he said.The envoy said food insecurity was fundamentally a consequence of conflict, political instability and underdevelopment, rather than their root cause. He called for greater cooperation among member states, international financial institutions, regional organisations and development partners to strengthen domestic agricultural production, diversify supply chains and improve storage and logistics infrastructure.âPredictable and affordable access to fertilisers, quality seeds, technology and concessional finance remains indispensable, particularly for developing countries. Open, transparent and rules-based trade in food and agricultural inputs also remains critical to global food security,â he said.India also cautioned against âover-reliance " on any single model of production, arguing that such dependence could leave food systems vulnerable to geopolitical disruptions, economic coercion and weaponisation.âWe must encourage small and marginal farmers to enhance their productivity and contribute to ensuring food security in developing countries of the Global South. We must also encourage climate-resilient crops such as millets rather than limit conceptions of food security to the biggest staple, grain crops such as rice, wheat and corn,â Parvathaneni said.Guterres said 2025 saw the highest number of armed conflicts since World War II alongside some of the highest levels of global acute hunger on record, with at least 266 million people facing acute food insecurity.He described the simultaneous confirmation of famine in Sudan and Gaza in 2025 as a âshameful milestoneâ, adding that conflict and violence were the primary drivers of hunger in 12 of the 13 hunger hotspots of greatest concern identified in the UNâs latest Hunger Hotspots report.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Lok Sabha Speaker seeks response from 20 rebel TMC MPs on disqualification petitions
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla has issued notices to 20 rebel Trinamool Congress (TMC) MPs who are now affiliated with the little-known Nationa.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla has issued notices to 20 rebel Trinamool Congress (TMC) MPs who are now affiliated with the little-known Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI), seeking their responses within seven days to disqualification petitions filed by the TMC.The disqualification petitions are currently pending before Birla.This comes after Solicitor General of India Tushar Mehta on Tuesday informed the Supreme Court that the Speaker had already issued notices to the 20 MPs on the disqualification petitions filed by the TMC under the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution.Mehta made the submission before a bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant while appearing for the Lok Sabha Speaker and the Secretary General of the House. The bench was hearing a plea filed by senior TMC leader Abhishek Banerjee, challenging the delay in deciding the petitions seeking the disqualification of the rebels.Responding to the submission, the bench said, "It is not a question of issuing notices, it is a question of concluding the proceedings within a time frame."During the hearing, the bench indicated that it was inclined to issue notices to the respondents on Abhishek Banerjeeâs writ petition. Mehta, however, submitted that there was no need to issue notices to the Speaker or his office, stating that he would appear on behalf of Birla.The TMC has accused the 20 MPs of âabandoningâ the party and subsequently joining the NCPI. Abhishek Banerjee has contended that their conduct attracts disqualification under the anti-defection provisions of the Constitution.The petition names the Lok Sabha Speaker and the Secretary General of the House as the principal respondents and also impleads the MPs whose disqualification is being sought.The respondents are Kakoli Ghosh Dastidar, Sudip Bandyopadhyay, Satabdi Roy, Prasun Banerjee, Rachana Banerjee, Jagadish Chandra Barma Basunia, Partha Bhowmick, Arup Chakraborty, Adhikari Deepak Dev, Sayani Ghosh, Bapi Haldar, Md Abu Taher Khan, Kalipada Saren Kherwal, Asit Kumar Mal, June Maliah, Mitali Bag, Khalilur Rahaman, Mala Roy, Sharmila Sarkar and Yusuf Pathan.(With ANI inputs)Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: BJP MLA's private Innova washed by fire brigade, video goes viral
articles.summary: SINGRAULI: A video purportedly showing a government fire brigade vehicle being used to wash the private Innova of a BJP MLA  outside his official resi.
articles.body: SINGRAULI: A video purportedly showing a government fire brigade vehicle being used to wash the private Innova of a BJP MLA outside his official residence in Madhya Pradesh's Singrauli has gone viral on social media, triggering questions over the alleged misuse of government resources.The video, reportedly recorded on Tuesday, shows a fire brigade vehicle parked outside the official residence of BJP MLA Ramniwas Shah in Bilounji.Three fire brigade personnel can be seen using a hose to spray water on an Innova car parked outside the residence.The vehicle is reportedly owned by Shah, who represents the Singrauli Assembly constituency (80).It is not clear why the fire brigade vehicle was present at the MLA's residence or under whose instructions the car was being washed.Neither Shah nor the concerned department has so far issued an official response to the video.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bhopal | Silver Rate in Bhopal | Bank Holidays in Bhopal | Public Holidays in Bhopal | Petrol Price in Bhopal | Diesel Price in Bhopal | CNG Price in Bhopal | LPG Price in BhopalStay updated with the latest Bhopal news. articles.title: Practical Magic 2's Kidman and Bullock board Essex vintage train
articles.summary: The stars appear on the train, specially transported to a film studos for a new movie sequel.
articles.body:
A call from Hollywood producers asking if film stars Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock could sit in a vintage railway carriage came out of the blue for station manager Robert Bentley.

They called him to ask if the duo could use it for their new blockbuster, Practical Magic 2, a sequel to the 1998 romantic fantasy tale.

While film producers were keen to feature it, they first needed the train moved from North Weald, Essex, to the Warner Bros Studios in Leavesden, Hertfordshire.

The studio filming left Bentley "in awe", he said. "When you're stood at the studio and then all of a sudden Sandra is stood next to you, it's hard to describe the feeling."

The 27-year-old said he ended up chatting to Bullock, who was interested in the history of the train.

Epping Ongar Railway has preserved its stations and carriages since closing in the 1990s.

Its authentic appearance has made it a popular go-to spot for film-makers, with it appearing in the TV shows Man vs Baby and Death in Paradise in recent times.

Bentley said producers had scouted around for locations before choosing to use North Weald station for a scene with US actress Joey King, as well as its train carriage, for filming last summer.

The final choice for Bullock's scene was a 1960s British Rail Mark 1 coach.

"We were the perfect fit for them in terms of what they wanted to film," said Bentley.

"We had the countryside and we had the coach that they wanted."

He said payment was not six digits, but "quite a high figure".

The film-makers also asked him to stick around for a scene, casting him as the train guard with a line of dialogue.

Other scenes were filmed at St Mary and All Saints Church in Lambourne, near Abridge.

The Grade I-listed church dates back to the 12th Century, but producers felt it could pass for a US church.

Last year, it was reported film and TV shows being made in Essex generated £3m for the local economy since 2022.

The Daniel Craig thriller Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery - filmed at a church in Epping Forest - has been among the productions providing a boost.

Essex County Council established the Essex Film Office in 2022 to attract more large film productions to the county.

It provides a point of contact for production companies looking for perfect filming locations - guiding them in the right direction and assisting them with permissions.

Manager Erica Gilson recalled feeling "hugely proud" to work on Mr Bates vs The Post Office, which included scenes at Shire Hall in Chelmsford.

She was emotional as she spoke about the impact it had.

"You're a tiny, tiny part in something that ends up having a huge difference, and that's the power of the arts," she said.

Jeff Bray, the council's cabinet member for regeneration, planning and heritage, said the county has "so much to offer" film studios.

"We've got everything: wide open countryside, fantastic beaches, heritage of every kind from Roman through to Medieval - whatever you want you'll find it here in Essex," he said.

articles.title: Kettering's Alfred East Art Gallery set to welcome visitors again
articles.summary: The Alfred East Art Gallery has been closed to the public for more than five years.
articles.body:
An art gallery will welcome visitors for the first time in more than five years by displaying a collection of work by local artists.

The Alfred East Art Gallery in Kettering, Northamptonshire, closed to the public in mid-2021 for redevelopment and later required extensive roof repairs following rain damage in 2023.

The gallery is part of a cultural hub, collectively known as Cornerstone, which also includes its library, museum and garden.

North Northamptonshire Council said that the new display, titled Prelude, would be located within the rear extension of the building from 5 September to 2 October ahead of the full reopening to coincide with Northamptonshire Day.

It will be the first exhibition to feature in the new Garden Room extension, with the Reform UK-controlled council stating the space would become "a flexible space for exhibitions, art workshops, and more".

The council said Prelude features work by six local artists "each with their own individual style".

Work by Charlotte Ashman, Samantha Brockway, Serena Durgheu, Rosie Jarvis, Simon Loach and Teresa Williams will be on show, with the council saying it would "bring painting, printmaking, collage and photography together in one space".

Greg Wilcox, the council's Reform UK executive member for communities, said: "This is an exciting moment for the team at the Alfred East Gallery, as well as residents.

"It will be great to see the site being used as it has always been intended – showcasing beautiful art."

Work to repair the Grade II-listed building has cost £4.8m, though was initially earmarked for a budget of up to £6.8m.

The Alfred East Art Gallery is named after Sir Alfred East, a famous landscape painter born in Kettering.

He was knighted in 1910 and served as president of the Royal Society of British Artists before his death in 1913.

articles.title: Europe’s gas prices are surging. Who will be the first to pay more?
articles.summary: Europe could face its toughest winter gas season since 2022 as wholesale prices trade near their highest level in more than three years. Household bills coul...
articles.body:
Gas and electricity bills could increase in Europe this winter if wholesale prices remain elevated long enough to feed through to consumers.

The benchmark European wholesale natural gas price, the Dutch front-month TTF, was trading at over €66 per megawatt-hour (MWh) later on Tuesday, down from above €68 earlier in the session. This compares with around €29/MWh at the beginning of the year.

The rally has been fuelled by growing investor concerns that the Strait of Hormuz could remain closed into the winter.

This comes at a time when the EU's gas-storage levels remain historically low ahead of the heating season.

EU gas storage was 62.99% full at the end of the gas day on 24 August, according to data from Gas Infrastructure Europe.

"Europe's gas stores are unusually low for the time of year," Natasha Fielding, editorial manager for gas, LNG, coal and biomass at Argus Media, told Euronews Business. She added that this level was far below the five-year average of 79%.

"The only other time in the last 15 years that stocks were close to as low was in 2021, ahead of the last major gas crisis," Fielding said.

Among the larger European markets with the lowest storage levels, Germany's stores were only 51% full, while those in the Netherlands stood at 44.3%.

Oxford Economics pointed out in a report published on 13 August — before the latest icrease in gas prices — that EU gas consumption is around 15%-20% lower than in 2021.

It said the EU can operate with lower storage levels, although that would mean relying on more winter LNG imports. And that could leave the EU more exposed to competition with Asian buyers for available cargoes.

The competition is already intensified due to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, disrupting a route that normally carries almost one-fifth of global LNG trade.

In a potential EU-Asia bidding war, wholesale prices could climb further.

At current levels, prices "will not be enough for Europe to manage storage through winter," Goldman Sachs analysts Samantha Dart and Laura Cyr wrote in a note cited by Bloomberg.

"In a scenario where Middle East energy exports normalise only gradually through 2027, we estimate that December 2026 TTF would likely need to move above €100/MWh," they said. That is 110% above Goldman's €50/MWh base case, they added.

Oxford Economics said the EU might be forced to suspend parts of its ban on Russian gas imports if supplies tightened further. According to the latest European Commission calculation, Russia's share of combined pipeline and LNG imports was around 12.5% in 2025.

articles.title: Muck-spreading: The smellier the better as farmers ask for patience
articles.summary: East Yorkshire farmers explain the process as they prepare their fields for next year's crops.
articles.body:
Farmers are asking people to be patient with the smell of manure as they spread it on their fields to prepare the land for next year's crops.

Muck-spreading is the process of distributing animal manure across farmland as a natural fertiliser and typically takes place twice a year, in spring and late summer.

Although "it might smell a bit", according to farmer Ben Clappison, from Cowlam, East Yorkshire, he says it is important as it helps improve the land and reduces the amount of chemical fertilisers.

He says: "[It helps] to make everything a lot healthier and improve soil organic matter and really push towards more organic fertilisers rather than inorganic."

Ben adds: "Our inorganics are manufactured fertilisers and a lot of raw products come from abroad. There's a lot of mileage on it, a lot of CO2 emitted in manufacturing it and it's expensive. Whereas this is coming out of the farm where it's produced."

Ben, who also spreads on other farmland as a contractor, says the process is carefully mapped out using the latest technology.

Manure from cattle, pigs and poultry is scooped from heaps in the fields and carefully weighed to be spread evenly.

Ben also uses human waste, known as sludge and taken from sewage works, to enrich the soil.

However, there are strict rules that farmers must follow when spreading sludge and Ben says he uses GPS to ensure it is only placed in the correct areas.

According to DEFRA, it can only be spread on crops that cannot be eaten directly from the land, such as wheat, barley and oil seed rape.

"We have a spreading app which has everything mapped out and all of the buffer zones and strips where you can't go anywhere near.

"We have to look after the fields, the soils, the environment because it has to be sustainable for not just my generation but generations to come."

The process can generate complaints from residents because of strong odours, although farmers say the smell is short-lived and an unavoidable part of food production.

Those unhappy with the smell can complain to the Environment Agency or their local authority.

However, as a rule, East Riding of Yorkshire Council says it is only likely to investigate if the smell is "particularly excessive or prolonged", adding "spreading manure on farmland is recognised as standard agricultural practice and odour can be expected from time to time".

The process, which takes place after a harvest, is seen as the first step in preparing the land for the next crop.

Angela Kirkwood, of the National Farmers' Union, says a strong smell is a sign of healthy soil.

"What we're trying to do is make the weeds grow so that we can get rid of those weeds but also incorporate that nutrient back into the soils to make the soil really good and healthy.

"We have a lot of soil testing that we do in order to look at what nutrients are already there and how we can improve the nutrients to make our crops grow and to make sure that we can continue producing food for everybody," she says.

"People just think of it as being a stinky process. And all farmers live it as well. Actually, the stinkier the muck, the better it is for the soil."

Angela advises residents to close their windows if they see muck-spreading taking place and not to put any washing out.

Although the smell cannot be helped, farmers say they do understand the complaints.

On Sunk Island in rural Holderness, arable farmer Jono Dixon says he is careful to reduce the impact of spreading chicken muck on his land near Patrington Haven Leisure Park.

He says: "We have the anxiety of spreading it because we know we're going to get the odd complaint, here there and everywhere, or from everybody.

"But this is a quick operation. We've seen in the other field, over there, where within 12 hours the lads are in behind ploughing all the chicken manure in.

"We are trying to do the best we can to not inconvenience people with what can be described as one hell of an odour."

articles.title: Witney designer wraps blanket heritage into fashion contest
articles.summary: Alexandra Burch takes her Cotswold Remnants collection to The Redress Design Award final in Hong Kong.
articles.body:
A young designer is highlighting local craftsmanship through her womenswear collection for an international fashion competition.

Alexandra Burch, 19, from Witney is among the eight finalists on the Redress Design Award , which challenges emerging designers to use certified textile waste for their creations.

Cotswold Remnants celebrates her hometown heritage of blanket making and is "entirely made from materials and offcuts salvaged from the Cotswold Woollen Weavers, a mill that sadly had to permanently close this year ".

She was flown out to Hong Kong on Sunday ahead of the grand final fashion show on 2 September.

She said she was "really excited" for her first visit to Asia, where she will face off with designers from all over the world.

"I know that some are from Austria, Germany, some are from Hong Kong and mainland China.

"We're all coming together, so I'm excited to meet everyone soon."

Alexandra said she would do fittings for the runway show models.

"I'm still very inspired by the 70s and the hippie movement but this collection ... was inspired by tweed jackets and traditional farmer wear in my local area, so I looked more locally this time."

Listen to the latest news from Oxfordshire

Her four-look collection was made of faulty tweed blankets and loom offcuts from the now closed mill in Filkins.

"It's all made of local British wool, undyed and naturally dyed," Alexandra said.

The designer, who is also a fashion design student at Kingston University, believes that "waste is not inevitable, it's a design decision".

"You should focus on sustainability at the start of your design, not add it on at the end.

"I think that true sustainability lies in valuing what already exists and designing for durability, so looking at the future."

The non-profit association Global Fashion Agenda , which aims to accelerate net-positive action in the industry, has found that "every year, 92 million tonnes of textile waste is produced globally".

The United Nations Environment Programme says this is the equivalent of "a garbage truck full of clothing being incinerated or sent to a landfill every second".

"I think at the moment the fashion industry is way out of hand, it's way too fast-paced and I think fast fashion brands must be held accountable," Alexandra said.

articles.title: 'Game changer' study seeks answers for heavy periods and endometriosis
articles.summary: It will the create world's largest menstrual fluid biobank to improve treatment of heavy periods.
articles.body:
A major new research project aiming to transform care for women with heavy periods is to create the world's largest menstrual fluid biobank.

The CycleTrack study hopes to improve understanding of heavy menstrual bleeding and related conditions such as endometriosis and fibroids, helping speed up diagnosis and treatment for millions of women.

Led by researchers from the universities of Bristol and Exeter, it will collect real-time health data and menstrual fluid samples from thousands of women across the UK.

Professor Gemma Sharp said the study was going to be "a real game changer" for menstrual health research and could cut waiting times for effective treatment.

As part of the study, researchers are working with women who have personal experience of heavy periods.

Maria Lewis, 34, from Weston-super-Mare, has lived with heavy menstrual bleeding since she first started menstruating and was diagnosed with endometriosis last year.

She has taken part in the Children of the 90s , external study since childhood and was keen to support the latest research.

Describing the impact of her condition, she said: "It's horrific. I'm in pain every day."

Although she cannot take part in the menstrual fluid collection because she takes hormonal contraception to manage her symptoms and no longer menstruates, she believes the research could help improve understanding of conditions affecting women.

She said: "Absolutely, it needs more of a platform and a louder voice."

Heavy menstrual bleeding, sometimes known as HMB, affects up to half of women worldwide and can have a significant impact on physical, emotional and social wellbeing.

Symptoms can include periods lasting more than seven days, the need to change sanitary protection every one to two hours, passing large blood clots and signs of iron deficiency such as fatigue and dizziness.

Researchers say menstrual health remains poorly understood despite being a key indicator of overall health, partly because of a lack of high-quality data.

Recent studies have suggested heavy periods can affect many aspects of daily life , external , including educational attainment and school attendance.

The study will recruit participants from two long-running birth cohort studies: Children of the 90s in south-west England and Born in Bradford in West Yorkshire.

Thousands of volunteers will use a specialist app and detailed questionnaires to record symptoms, sleep, mood, energy levels and overall wellbeing.

Participants will also provide menstrual fluid samples over three menstrual cycles using specially designed period pads.

By linking those samples with long-term health information and genetic data already held by the cohort studies, researchers hope to uncover biological signals associated with heavy menstrual bleeding.

They believe the findings could lead to earlier diagnosis, more personalised treatment plans and new methods of identifying health risks linked to heavy periods, including iron deficiency.

The project is being led by Sharp, an epidemiologist at the University of Exeter who specialises in women's health research.

She said: "HMB is excessive menstrual blood loss that interferes with your physical, social, emotional and/or quality of life.

"It can occur with or without underlying pathology such as fibroids, hormonal issues.

"Common symptoms can often include: bleeding lasting longer than seven days, needing to change protection every one to two hours, passing large clots, signs of iron deficiency anaemia (e.g. fatigue, dizziness)."

The study is part of a wider international programme known as The Missed Vital Sign, , external led by Wellcome Leap, which aims to dramatically reduce the time women wait for effective treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding.

Professor Sharp said CycleTrack would be the largest bank of dried menstrual fluid samples in the world.

She added: "We'll be able to understand what causes different conditions, like endometriosis, fibroids, the impact of those conditions on other areas of life, and then hopefully new ways to predict, prevent, and treat those symptoms as well."

Researchers say the work could help address long-standing gaps in understanding menstrual health and improve support for millions of women.

Although periods are experienced by around half the population during their lifetime, campaigners and health experts have often argued menstrual health has not received the same level of research attention as many other areas of medicine.

The CycleTrack , external team hopes the large volume of data generated by the study will provide new insights into how heavy periods affect everyday life, work, education and general health.

The information could also help shape future guidance for schools and employers on supporting people affected by heavy menstrual bleeding.

Scientists say many women face delays in diagnosis and treatment, while some may not realise symptoms such as extreme tiredness or dizziness can be linked to blood loss and iron deficiency.

By analysing biological samples alongside day-to-day symptom information, the team hopes to identify markers that could eventually help clinicians recognise problems sooner and tailor treatment more effectively.

Sample collection is due to begin this month, with researchers expecting data from thousands of participants to contribute to what they describe as a step change in understanding menstrual health.

All the data will have been collected by end of November 2027. Preliminary findings will follow by early 2028.

Currently only Children of the 90s and Born in Bradford participants can take part, but the research team has a waiting list , external if people are interested in taking part in future studies (funding dependent).

articles.title: Lunar Eclipse on Raksha Bandhan 2026: Will sutak affect Rakhi Rituals? Can you tie rakhi normally in India?
articles.summary: Rituals & Puja News: Raksha Bandhan 2026 comes with an unusual celestial coincidence. On August 28, the same day as Raksha Bandhan, a deep partial lunar eclipse will take .
articles.body: Raksha Bandhan 2026 comes with an unusual celestial coincidence. On August 28, the same day as Raksha Bandhan, a deep partial lunar eclipse will take place. At its peak, more than 90% of the Moon will enter Earthâs umbral shadow.Naturally, this has created one big question:Should you change your Rakhi rituals because of Chandra Grahan?For people celebrating Raksha Bandhan in India, the short answer is: No, not simply because an eclipse is happening somewhere on Earth.The Most Important Detail: The Eclipse Is Not Visible in IndiaThis is where much of the confusion begins.The lunar eclipse takes place on August 28, but it will not be visible from India. During the eclipse, the Moon will already be below the horizon here.This distinction is important from a traditional perspective as well.In many commonly followed Dharmic traditions, Grahan-related observances and Sutak are associated with the visibility of the eclipse at a particular location. Therefore, if you are celebrating Raksha Bandhan in India, you do not need to automatically observe eclipse-related Sutak merely because the astronomical eclipse falls on the same date.So, Can You Tie Rakhi Normally in India?Yes.If you are in India, the eclipse itself does not require you to cancel Raksha Bandhan, postpone Rakhi, stop the puja, or treat the entire day as inauspicious.Your Rakhi timing should instead be decided according to Purnima Tithi, Bhadra, local sunrise, and the appropriate Raksha Bandhan Muhurta, as you would normally do.This is an important distinction:An eclipse existing astronomically and an eclipse being ritually applicable at your location are not necessarily the same thing.So, don't allow a social-media headline saying âChandra Grahan on Raksha Bandhanâ to create unnecessary fear.Does the Eclipse Still Have Astrological Significance?This is where we need to separate ritual rules from astrological interpretation.The planetary alignment of August 28 places the Moon in Aquarius, while Rahu is also positioned in Aquarius. On the opposite side, the Sun, Mercury, and Ketu strongly activate Leo, while Jupiter remains exalted in Cancer.So, astrologically, this is certainly an interesting Raksha Bandhan.The larger theme is not fear. It is about relationships, emotional patterns, family roots, individuality, and protection.Rakhi itself is a festival built around Rakshaâthe conscious promise of protection. So, instead of becoming anxious about Grahan, use the occasion to look at the sibling relationship beyond photographs, sweets, and gifts.Has distance quietly entered the relationship?Is there something unresolved between you?Are you protecting your sibling, or sometimes trying to control them?Is an old family disagreement still being carried unnecessarily?Those questions are far more useful than becoming frightened simply because the word Grahan appears on the calendar.Get the latest religion news and spiritual insights. articles.title: RSPB reports record-breaking Cornish chough numbers
articles.summary: RSPB England says 161 Choughs have been counted - 32 more than the 129 recorded last year.
articles.body:
A record-breaking number of choughs have made their nests around the Cornish coastline this summer, proving the breed is in "robust health", a bird conservation charity has said.

RSPB England said 161 choughs had been counted in Cornwall - 32 more than the 129 recorded in 2025 .

The charity said the new birds came from 56 successful breeding pairs, meaning the average productivity of a Cornish chough nest was three fledglings.

It said choughs died out in Cornwall in the 1970s but returned in 2001 when three birds believed to be from Ireland landed at Lizard Point and began rebreeding. The National Trust added the success had been down to cooperation between agencies, farmers and landowners.

The birds, part of the carrion crow family, have a particular significance in Cornwall, featuring on the county's official coat of arms, alongside a miner and a fisherman.

Peter Hall, a National Trust chough monitoring volunteer on the Lizard, is in his 11th year of monitoring the nest sites.

He said he had not foreseen a time when he would be monitoring so many sites -"certainly not having 16 choughlets fledge".

Hall said: "The past two winters we have been blessed with chatterings in excess of 20 chough around the Lizard - a far cry from the solitary single pair we had when I started as part of the then nest protection team in 2016.

"Long may the successful return of this iconic Cornish bird delight myself and others."

The charity said the Lizard was the prime breeding ground for the Cornish chough, with 26 chicks, 11 more than 2025, emerging from eight nests on the peninsula.

National Trust volunteer Lydia Allt said 2026 had been "an exceptional one" for choughs on the Lizard and across Cornwall.

She said: "Thanks to a quarter of a century of conservation work, partnership working and the support of local farmers and land managers, we are seeing record numbers ofchough across the area.

"Their remarkable recovery shows what can be achieved when habitats are restored and protected, giving wildlife the space it needs to thrive.

"To see so many choughs successfully breeding and feeding across the Lizard is incredibly encouraging and highlights the importance of continuing to care for this special landscape for future generations."

Andrew Jones, chough conservation officer for the RSPB in Cornwall, said the repopulation work would not be possible without volunteers.

He said: "There has been a huge volunteer effort over the past 25 years to protect and monitor Cornwall's iconic choughs and we're grateful to everyone who has played their part in this conservation success story.

"This year, the RSPB and National Trust have had a team of around 50 dedicated volunteer chough watchers, covering the coastline from the Roseland all the way round to Bude, monitoring the breeding efforts and reporting back so we could collate these fantastic, record-breaking numbers."

articles.title: Chloe Moffat: Dad of woman who took her own life says Treasury failed in its duty of care
articles.summary: Chloe Moffat died last year, after she was told of allegations she had shared sensitive confidential information about colleagues, which she denied.
articles.body:
The father of a civil service employee who took her own life the day after a meeting with her managers has said the lack of support given to her by the Treasury "beggars belief".

Chloe Moffat, 26, a personal assistant to a Treasury director, died on 20 May last year, after she was told of allegations she had shared sensitive confidential information about colleagues, which she denied.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, David Moffat said he did not feel the Treasury had taken responsibility for its part in her death.

He added that her loss was "devastating", and had "torn such a big hole in our lives".

The Treasury said "it will learn the lessons from this tragedy".

On 19 May 2025, Chloe went to what she thought was a routine one-to-one with her line manager, but a more senior manager was also present.

"Chloe's first comment was, 'Oh, this must be serious, there's two of you here'", David told Today's Emma Barnett. "So that's the first time that she was aware of anything [that] might be a to do."

"And then they worked through and put several allegations to her that she'd shared confidential information."

During the meeting, David said she had asked on several occasions if she would lose her job, and if she could have a friend there - both of which were refused.

A coroner found at an inquest earlier in August that the Treasury did not apply written disciplinary policy, which would have made clear that if the allegations against Chloe were proven, the likely penalty was a written warning, not dismissal.

"Even though she asked, they said they could not determine the outcome," David said.

Straight after the meeting, Chloe was locked out of her emails. "That was all part of the shock and awe of it all for Chloe," David said.

The coroner found that the meeting between Chloe and her managers "materially contributed" to her death.

Treasury contributed to woman's death, inquest hears

David said that "there wasn't any duty of care" shown to Chloe by the Treasury.

"There was no safeguarding, there was no support during or after that meeting, from what we've seen and what we've read", he said.

"It beggars belief that an organisation that is front and central in our government cannot get it right."

Asked whether he felt the Treasury had taken responsibility for its part in her death, he answered: "Not yet".

He added, however, that he and his wife had received a letter on Tuesday from the Treasury's permanent secretary, James Bowler, and that they had also met him last August.

David said while they could not change what happened to Chloe, he wanted "to ensure" that "lessons are learned".

"If something positive can come from this unbearable loss that we're suffering, that's all we look to achieve."

He said he and his wife Anne were unsure if they would be pursuing further action against the Treasury, but that they wanted "redress".

"We will learn the lessons from this tragedy. We are working urgently to respond to the coroner's findings and we have introduced immediate changes to our guidance, support and wellbeing arrangements.

He added that her loss was "devastating", and had "torn such a big hole in our lives".

articles.title: At least 15 newborns die in Pakistan hospital fire
articles.summary: At least 15 newborn babies died in a fire at a maternity ward in Pakistan's capital Islamabad, local rescue officials told dpa on Wednesday. The fire was lik...
articles.body:
At least 15 newborn babies died in a fire at a maternity ward in Pakistan's capital Islamabad, local rescue officials told dpa on Wednesday.

The fire was likely caused by a malfunctioning air conditioning unit in the early hours of the morning, the officials said.

Only one of the newborns in the ward was rescued, they said. The fire was now under control.

The maternity ward is part of the gynaecology department at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS), a state-run hospital. At least 16 newborns were in the nursery when the fire broke out.

Television footage from Geo News showed heavy smoke and firefighters working at the scene. The broadcaster said an investigation would be launched into the further causes of the fire.

Public hospitals in Pakistan are unpopular because of lower standards, with those who can afford it opting for private clinics for better care. Lax safety standards have repeatedly led to tragedies in Pakistan.

articles.title: Channel Islands on course for 'hottest ever summer'
articles.summary: Guernsey and Jersey are set to have seen the warmest summer ever, says the Met Office.
articles.body:
The summer of 2026 is on course to be the Channel Islands' hottest since records began, according to local meteorologists.

Provisional statistics from Jersey Met show Jersey's average temperature, measured across both day and night, was 20.9C (69.6F) between 1 June and 15 August. That is 3.2C (5.8F) above the 1991 to 2020 average.

Guernsey's mean temperature over the same period, and with two weeks of summer to go, is 19.2°C (66.56F), some 3C (5.4F) above the average, meteorologists said.

It was in line with evidence that climate change was driving hotter summers and increasing the likelihood of drier conditions, they added.

There have also been record-breaking temperatures across the islands, with Guernsey reaching 36.4°C (97.52F) on 25 June, its highest temperature ever recorded; and Jersey reaching 39.3°C (102.74F) on the same day, also its highest temperature on record.

Alongside the summer heat, the islands have experienced significantly lower than average rainfall.

In Jersey, 69.6mm of rain fell over the summer, compared with a 30-year average of 158.0mm.

In Guernsey, 43.2mm of rain was recorded, well below the 30-year average of 147.6mm.

Unlike large parts of the UK, this lack of rain has not led to drought conditions or hosepipe band across the islands.

Paul Aked, from Jersey Met, said the summer had not been too dissimilar to famous drought of 1976 , although 2026 had actually been hotter, with more heatwave periods and higher peak temperatures.

Aked went on to say, in terms of the heat and how people felt it: "It is very different for the islands when we're comparing ourselves with a city in the United Kingdom.

"We have the sea around us, which is cooler than the air temperature, and that does influence [where we] get some cooling from."

He added: "Just because we've had a hot summer, it doesn't mean we're going to get a particularly cold or wet or wintry winter."

articles.title: 'Very close call' as fire nearly hits Jersey Water plant
articles.summary: Firefighters tackle flames which were near to Jersey Water's desalination plant in Corbiere.
articles.body:
A large fire came "dangerously close" to a desalination plant, water bosses have said.

Jersey Water said the incident which was tackled by the island's firefighters in a nearby field in Corbiere on Monday highlighted the stark risks posed by wildfires in the current dry conditions.

It said if the plant, which turns sea water into drinking water, had been damaged, Jersey would have lost "critical resilience" to the island's water supply during prolonged periods of dry weather.

The utility company said it was "extremely grateful" to Jersey Fire Service, its own staff and the public for acting quickly to protect the plant.

Jersey Fire Service said 18 firefighters went to the scene after a bonfire lit in a dry field was spread by strong winds.

It issued a warning against people lighting fires in the open as conditions across the island remained "very dry".

Jersey Water echoed the fire service's warning and said people should take extra care and avoid activities which could start a fire.

"This incident was certainly a very close call and a stark reminder of the risks posed by wildfire," a company spokesperson said.

"The desalination plant is a vital part of Jersey's drought response.

"Had it been damaged, we would have lost critical resilience for the island's water supply during prolonged dry periods."

articles.title: PSNI officer sacked after investigation finds 'catalogue of corruption'
articles.summary: A Police Ombudsman investigation found the constable failed to disclose multiple conflicts of interest, intimidated a former partner, attempted to falsify evidence and asked a colleague to lie.
articles.body:
A Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) officer has been dismissed after an investigation found he initiated a sexual relationship with a woman he met in the course of his duties.

A Police Ombudsman inquiry also found he failed to disclose multiple conflicts of interest, intimidated a former partner, attempted to falsify evidence and asked a colleague to lie.

Ombudsman Jacqui Durkin said the behaviour was a "catalogue of corruption" which had "the potential to do serious damage to public trust and confidence in policing".

The PSNI said the officer's behaviour was "unacceptable and clearly falls far below the standards the public rightly expects at all times from police officers and staff".

Durkin said the officer, known in the investigation as Police Officer B, was a constable "of some experience" and that the allegations he faced was "one of the most serious types of police corruption".

She added that there was "no place for him, or any other officer, in the PSNI who misconducts himself in this way".

"This should send out a clear message to any other officers who may be involved in that type of behaviour that the consequences are that you will be dismissed."

Abuse of position for sexual purposes (APSP) cases currently account for 36% of the most serious cases currently under investigation by the Police Ombudsman's Office.

Investigators at the Police Ombudsman's office spent almost two years working through, what Durkin described as a "very complex, multi-stranded investigation".

Following the completion of the Police Ombudsman's investigation, a file was submitted to the Public Prosecution Service who issued a no prosecution decision in October 2024.

The case stemmed from an assault allegation made to the police by one woman, Woman A, against another, Woman B, who then made a counter assault allegation, in 2018.

The police officer responsible for investigating the incident, Police Officer A, asked a colleague, Police Officer B, to take a statement from Woman B.

Police Officer B, did not disclose that he had been in a sexual relationship with Woman A in 2016 and was still in contact with her socially.

Within 24 hours of meeting Woman B to take her statement, he had contacted her through Facebook and Snapchat and then began a sexual relationship with her.

A short time later they were living together and had a child before their relationship ended in early 2020.

The investigation also extended to a further incident in 2021 when another woman who had been in a relationship with Police Officer B reported that she had received a threatening, anonymous letter.

The letter was sent a short time after Police Officer B had been made aware that he was being investigated for his contact with vulnerable women.

It included an intimate photograph of the woman and also made threats that more photos would be sent to her family.

The only person she had shared the photo with was her former boyfriend, Police Officer B.

Two weeks before she received the letter, she had also received a phone notification that he had downloaded all the images she had shared.

When examined, the police officer's phone contained 51 images of the woman including intimate photos similar to the one she had received anonymously through the post.

The PSNI held a misconduct hearing in April and the officer was dismissed without notice.

The panel found that the officer had misconducted himself by breaching the PSNI Code of Ethics.

Police Officer B was the seventh officer to be dismissed as a result of Police Ombudsman investigations in APSP since 2020.

A further police officer received a written final warning.

In Northern Ireland, there is no specific 'misconduct in public office' offence. It is, instead, a common law offence.

Durkin hopes that the new Public Office (Accountability) Bill that is going through parliament will create a specific misconduct in public office offence.

She also welcomed the development of the Justice Bill that is making its way through the Northern Ireland Assembly.

"[This will] fast track some of those cases so that we would no longer have to wait until the conclusion of a decision to prosecute," she said.

This way, she explained, where there is "clear evidence of misconduct", the police can decide whether they dismiss an officer based on the evidence-led ombudsman investigation.

"Where you have predatory police officers, it's important that victims or complainants... can be assured of evidence led, impartial and independent investigation".

Chief Superintendent Stephen Murray, Head of the PSNI's professional standards department, said the serious misconduct identified in this case was "unacceptable and clearly falls far below the standards the public rightly expects, at all times, from police officers and staff".

"Police officers are entrusted with significant powers and responsibilities. That trust must never be abused for personal or sexual gain.

"Abuse of position for sexual purposes is wholly unacceptable, it is a serious abuse of authority and a breach of the trust placed in policing by the public.

"The behaviour found in this case was simply intolerable. It involved failures to declare conflicts of interest, dishonesty and conduct which undermined the integrity, impartiality and professionalism expected of every police officer."

The dismissal without notice, he added, reflected how serious the organisation took these matters "and reinforces our position that there is no place for corruption or abuse of position for sexual purposes in policing".

articles.title: Fermanagh barn owl success raises hopes for rare bird
articles.summary: Ten chicks have been successfully reared by two breeding pairs at secret sites across Fermanagh.
articles.body:
Barn owls have had a bumper summer in County Fermanagh, with 10 chicks recorded across two sites.

The breeding success follows years of conservation work by Ulster Wildlife with local farmers installing nest boxes and improving habitat for the elusive bird.

There are thought to be fewer than 30 breeding pairs left in Northern Ireland. The chicks have had rings placed on their legs so that they can be recorded in any other areas they turn up in after leaving the nest.

People are being encouraged to report any sightings of barn owls across Northern Ireland, particularly in the west, to help fill in gaps in the records and even help protect important breeding areas.

The Fermanagh chicks are thought to be the first recorded ones in the county for half a century.

Most of Ulster Wildlife's barn owl records come from the east of Northern Ireland.

The two broods of five chicks appeared in nest boxes that had been installed at different sites, after more than a decade of work with landowners.

The locations are being kept secret to help protect the rare, locally endangered bird.

Katy Bell, a senior conservation officer from Ulster Wildlife, said nest boxes play a part, but the willingness of farmers to adapt to the needs of the "magical, mystical" barn owl has been important too.

"We've been working closely with landowners, advising on land management and also putting up boxes," she said.

"So it's the combination of both - really you need nice thick hedgerows, lots of kind of rough areas and long grass for them to hunt over and then somewhere for them to nest. And that's really exciting."

The charity has worked closely with BirdWatch Ireland and has seen the population start to spread up from County Cavan.

The chicks have had small identification rings placed round their legs so that they can be traced when they are spotted again.

It is the first time chicks are known to have been ringed in Fermanagh under licence from the Northern Ireland Environment Agency, with support from the British Trust for Ornithology.

Over the past 50 years, barn owl numbers have declined across the UK.

The birds are now red-listed - classified as being at risk of extinction - largely due to a loss of habitat but also the use of pesticide.

Bell has been closely involved in the project to support barn owls.

"They face so many challenges," Bell said.

"They get poisoned with rodenticides, the loss of trees for them to nest in, the loss of nice big hedgerows for them to hunt over, the loss of rough ground for them to hunt over. They do get hit on our roads.

"They're just really up against it, so anything that we can do to create little safe havens for them here Is just they really need."

Those safe havens come in the form of nest boxes, specially designed to resemble the tree cavities barn owls nest in that are disappearing from our countryside.

Conservationists can access the nests to check on any chicks and ensure their wellbeing.

And there is a platform on the front, where the young birds will exercise and practise flying before leaving the nest.

Bell has "a long, long list" of farmers applying to have boxes installed.

"Of course, they're the farmer's friend - if you have them on the farm, that's free rodent control.

"They're eating your rats and your mice and everything on your farm.

"They work in harmony with us, which is just wonderful."

They usually nest in cavities that form in large, old trees like oaks.

And they need to be near rough ground that offers habitat for the small rodents they hunt.

But the number of the right type of tree near the right type of area is falling.

Bell said suburban back gardens are just not suitable.

"We either need barns - we put some in barns - or big, mature trees and open ground.

"So usually we go out and visit farms in the autumn, see if they're suitable and then if they are, we'll put up boxes in the winter time."

But people can still play a part in supporting barn owls by reporting sightings.

And Bell said the birds are a sight that cannot be forgotten.

They're actually quite small birds, about the size of a wood pigeon, but they look much bigger - they have a wingspan much bigger in comparison to most other birds to their body size.

"So you see them hovering over the field and you'll get this just big flash of white.

"And it's just like nothing else you'll see."

articles.title: Fermanagh barn owl success raises hopes for rare bird
articles.summary: Ten chicks have been successfully reared by two breeding pairs at secret sites across Fermanagh.
articles.body:

articles.title: US embassies across the world to visa applicants: Your visa application is on hold as our consular officers need to be ...
articles.summary: Tech News News: Immigrant visa applicants across the world have been told that their applications are on hold as the Trump administration has launched a global traini.
articles.body: Immigrant visa applicants across the world have been told that their applications are on hold as the Trump administration has launched a global training initiative for consular officers. According to a report by Financial Times, the scheduled interviews at US embassies and consulates are now being rescheduled and the applicants are also receiving notices that the new dates will be provided later. A State Department spokesperson said the pause is meant to ensure officers can âevaluate every visa applicant comprehensively and consistently.â The training emphasizes screening out individuals deemed likely to become a public charge, or dependent on U.S. public benefits. âA more prosperous America means ensuring that visa applicants are not likely to become a public charge,â the spokesperson told the Financial Times.Why US embassies are emailing immigrant visa applicantsUS embassies and consulates have begun emailing immigrant visa applicants to inform them that their scheduled interview appointments are being rescheduled, with no new date provided â only a promise of future notice once a new time is set. The disruption is affecting applicants globally, from Mumbai to Naples, many of whom had already made costly, time-sensitive arrangements to attend their original appointments.The State Department's explanationA State Department spokesperson told the Financial Times the pause is tied to a newly launched "global training initiative" intended to ensure consular officers are fully equipped to evaluate every visa applicant comprehensively and consistently. The stated goal centers on public-charge screening â filtering out applicants deemed likely to become dependent on US public benefits. The spokesperson framed the effort as part of ensuring prosperity for the country by keeping out those unlikely to be self-sufficient under US law.The department did not offer a timeline for when appointments would resume, saying only that visa service scheduling would be adjusted to accommodate the training.Part of a broader immigration crackdownThe pause is the latest in a series of moves by an administration that has made restricting entry to the US a defining priority. President Trump has centered his presidency on cracking down on undocumented immigration while also tightening legal pathways â imposing new limits on visas and green cards and effectively ending nearly all refugee resettlement.The pause comes just days after a federal judge struck down a related Trump administration policy that had barred immigrant visa applications from nationals of 75, mostly lower-income, countries the administration considered likely to require public assistance. US District Judge Jeannette Vargas ruled that the ban â announced by the State Department in January â exceeded the administration's authority by overriding the discretion Congress assigned to consular officers in visa decision-making. Vargas struck down the policy along with any visa refusals issued under it, and gave both sides until September 11 to propose next steps in the litigation.The sequence has left some immigration attorneys questioning whether the new "training" pause is, functionally, a way to continue restricting the same pool of applicants after the original policy was struck down in court â though the State Department has not characterised it that way.The dilemma of visa applicantsAs per the FT report, Brian Simmons, an attorney at immigration law firm Fragomen in Washington, said many affected applicants had already spent thousands of dollars and upended their lives to attend interviews that were then canceled at the last minute. The disruption is especially acute for a specific group: since last year, the administration has required immigrant visa applicants to process their cases in their country of citizenship â even when they already live and work legally in the US, and even when they are married to American citizens or have American children. For that population, a canceled appointment can mean an extended, unplanned stay abroad, separated from family, jobs, and homes back in the US.Legal context: A long history of court battlesThis isn't the first time Trump's immigration policies have run into judicial pushback. Early in his first term, federal courts rolled back his attempt to bar entry to nationals of seven majority-Muslim countries, before the Supreme Court eventually allowed a scaled-back version of that policy to proceed. The current litigation over the 75-country visa ban suggests a similar legal fight may be ahead for whatever policy ultimately replaces or follows this new global pause.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.
